fetched_contents.text: Recent advances in bioactive peptides from fermented plant-based foods and their bioactivities Abstract Bioactive peptides (BAPs), which are protein fragments defined by their distinct structural features and amino acid sequences, impart health benefits to foods enriched with them. These benefits include antioxidant, antihypertensive, antidiabetic, and immunomodulatory properties. BAPs have emerged as potential substitutes for synthetic molecules in various applications. Nevertheless, there is inadequate of information on the production of BAPs via novel fermented plant-based foods (FPFs), and many BAPs resources in FPFs have not been effectively explored. This review extensively discussed recent trends in FPFs, ranging from vinegar, cheese liquor, fermented rice, etc., from 2019 to 2024. We further discuss the beneficial health impacts of BAPs derived from FPFs, factors affecting the bioavailability of bioactive peptides, trends, and future perspectives in bioactive compounds from fermentation foods. This review will add to the existing body of knowledge and improve our understanding of the potential of BAPs derived from fermented plant-based foods. Keywords: Bioactive peptides, Beneficial health effects, Fermentation, Functional foods, Nutraceuticals Graphical abstract Highlights * • Plant-based fermented foods’ (FPFs) peptides in the last 5 years were reviewed. * • Bioactive peptides (BAPs) from FPFs show promise of therapeutic benefits. * • FPFs are a direct and high-quality source for BAPs. * • BAPs are potent, low-risk alternatives to synthetic ingredients in nutraceuticals and functional foods. * • The current trends and future perspectives for BAPs from FPFs are discussed. 1. Introduction The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) projected that by 2050, the world population is expected to reach close to 9 billion people (Garrido-Galand et al., 2021), with such an increase in population, the food industry and researchers have been focusing on the utilization of fermentation to improve human diet by further exploring efficient and sustainable alternatives to satisfy the demand on the food market (Rogers et al., 2024). Currently, people tend to believe that food contributes to health and that medical issues are closely related to the food consumed (Anosike et al., 2022). Since 8000 BC, fermentation has been used in human nutrition. Traditionally, fermentation has been used for food preservation, flavor improvement, and nutritional value addition (Rastogi et al., 2022). This method has been explored as an effective way to increase the synthesis of microbial metabolites with biological properties, utilizing a variety of substrates to accomplish various functional benefits such as antioxidant, antidiuretic, and antihypertensive actions (Sharma et al., 2020). Globally, fermented food accounts for approximately one-third of the food consumed and 20–40% (by weight) of individual diets (Campbell-Platt, 1994; Campbell-Platt, 2014). Fermented plant-based foods encompass those derived from cereals, vegetables (sauerkraut), soy (miso and natto), etc. Notable secondary metabolites, including peptides, are produced during fermentation. These bioactive compounds exert several biological activities, among which are chronic disease prevention, such as cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and cancer (Chang et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2023). Fermented food products, particularly those made from soy, chickpeas, and cereals, have been acknowledged in East and Southeast Asia as sizable food sources that have had a massive effect on dietary life (Romulo & Surya, 2021). Throughout fermentation, secondary metabolic pathways may result in the production of bioactive compounds or enzymes that liberate bioactive compounds from the substrate, which are beneficial to humans and animals (Durazzo et al., 2022). Beneficial bioactive compounds from various meals, including bioactive peptides, impact biological functions and cellular activity, for instance treating metabolic disorders like hypertension, hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, and obesity (Chen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2023). Bioactive substances, such as antimicrobial peptides, act as secondary metabolites during fermentation. These substances include phenyl lactic acid and hydroxyphenyl acetic acid, indoleacetic acid, alcohols such as phenylethyl alcohol, and indoleacetic acid (Ma et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024). These bioactive substances significantly influence the bio-preservation of fermented food products such as cheese, beer, sourdough, and fermented vegetables (Guo et al., 2025). Enhancing the extraction of bioactive compounds and increasing their bioactivity in food has become a fascinating area of research for scientists in recent times (Tolve et al., 2021), not only for the health benefits of these bioactive compounds but also for their aromatic quality, which is known to affect the sensory and organoleptic qualities of food products, particularly the flavor and fragrance qualities of fermented plant-based foods (Sorrenti et al., 2023). Furthermore, it has been discovered that combining multiple bioactive compounds can produce a synergistic effect, resulting in greater bioactivity and functionality than a single component (Gao et al., 2022). A single micro-delivery system for probiotic strains and bioactive compounds in the targeted colon through food products has the potential to develop by this generally accepted idea in the pharmaceutical business (Shah et al., 2023). BAPs have emerged as potential substitutes for synthetic molecules in various applications, primarily due to their minimal adverse effects and significant value in the nutraceutical and functional food industry. fetched_contents.text: Structure and Function of Human Matrix Metalloproteinases Abstract The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a macromolecules network, in which the most abundant molecule is collagen. This protein in triple helical conformation is highly resistant to proteinases degradation, the only enzymes capable of degrading the collagen are matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs). This resistance and maintenance of collagen, and consequently of ECM, is involved in several biological processes and it must be strictly regulated by endogenous inhibitors (TIMPs). The deregulation of MMPs activity leads to development of numerous diseases. This review shows MMPs complexity. Keywords: matrix metalloproteinases, TIMP, collagen 1. Extracellular Matrix—Collagen The extracellular matrix (ECM) is a macromolecules network, composed of collagen, enzymes and proteins (Figure 1), that promote a structural and biochemical support. The ECM has many components [1]: Fibers (collagen, elastin, laminin, and fibronectin), proteoglycans (syndecan-1 and aggrecan), glycoproteins (tenascin, vitronectin and entactin) and polysaccharides (hyaluronic acid) [2], that regulate cell migration, growth, and differentiation [3]. The collagen is the most abundant protein in ECM which gives structural support for cells [1,3]. Depending of mineralization degree, the tissues can be divided in rigid (bones) or compliant (sinews) or have a gradient between these two states (cartilage) [4]. Collagen can come in two main forms: fibrillar (type I, II, III, V, and XI) and non-fibrillar, the latter includes facit-fibril associated collagens with interrupted triple helix (type IX, XII, XIV, XIX, and XXI); short chain (type VIII and X); basement membrane (type IV); multiplexin (type XV and XVIII); MACIT- membrane associated collagens with interrupted triple-helix (type XIII and XVII) and others types (Type VI, VII, and VIII). The collagen protein consists of three α chains, in triple helix, where two chains are chemically similar (α1 and α2), with approximate dimensions of 300 × 1.5 nm [3,5]. The triple helix is divided into five d-segments with D1–D4 having a length of 67 nm and D5 equal to 0.46 nm [3,5]. The high glycine content is important for collagen helix stabilization as it allows collagen fibers to combine, facilitating hydrogen bridges and cross-link formation [5]. The collagen synthesis involves several steps [5] (Figure 2). The mRNA is transcripted by ribosome, forming pre-propeptide. The following three stages occur in the endoplasmic reticulum: (1) The N-terminal signal sequence is removed; (2) hydroxylation of lysine and proline by prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylases takes place, together with (3) glycosylation of lysine, forming the pro-collagen. This structure is a triple helix chain, but with the unwound terminals. The removal of these terminals occurs in extracellular medium, by collagen peptidases, forming tropocollagen. The microfibril collagen is formed by lysyl oxidase that packs together five tropocollagen chain [3], which have a characteristic image. At intervals of 67 nm, one zone has the roll of all tropocollagen and another zone has one less—“gap”. The fibril collagen is composed of various microfibril collagen group and the alternating overlap and gap regions create the characteristic “bright and dark” d-banding pattern [3]. Its triple helix conformation makes collagen resistant to many proteases. The enzymes able to cleave this structure are capthesin K and enzymes with collagenolytic activity (MMPs-1, -2, -8, -13, -14, and -18) [3,4]. The collagen type I, II and III have a specific cleavage sequence: (Gln/Leu)-Gly#(Ile/Leu)-(Ala/Pro), which is located at 3/4 of N-terminal and this is crucial for collagen degradation [6,7] (Figure 3). The denatured collagen is called gelatin, which can be further degraded by gelatinases [4,6]. The collagen degradation is involved in many biological processes, such as embryogenesis, morphogenesis, tissue remodulation, angiogenesis, and wound healing [4]. The ECM degradation is also an important process in development, morphogenesis, tissue repair and remodulation [8], and can affect the cellular behavior and phenotype [6,9]. The excessive degradation of ECM leads to metabolic and immune diseases, cancer and cardiovascular disorders (hypertension, atherosclerosis and aneurysm) [2,3,6]. 2. Metzincs Superfamily—Matrix Metalloproteinases (MMPs) The metzincs are a family of multidomain zinc-dependent endopeptidases, where the metalloproteinases such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) [10], the desintegrins and metalloproteins (ADAMS), the ADAMs with thrombospondin motif (ADAMTS), were snapalysins, leishmanolysins, pappalysins belong [1,6,8,11,12,13,14]. All of them have a common conserved domain: HExxHxxGxxH [6,11,12,13,15,16,17,18,19] and, in case for MMPs, this sequence is HEBGHxLGLxHSBMxP [13]. The MMPs were first described in 1949 [20], as depolymerizing enzymes that facilitate tumor growth, by making connective tissue stroma, including small blood vessels that are more fluid [16,20,21]. In 1962, a MMP collagenase was isolated and characterized as an enzyme responsible for tadpole tail resorption [1,2,6,13,14,16,21,22], by Gross and Lapiere [22]. Over the next 20 years, several enzymes were purified, but it was in 1985 that the area has developed more significantly [16,21]. Taken together it has been demonstrated that MMPs are present in virus, archeabacteria, bacteria, plants, nematodes, and animals [6,13]. The MMPs are a family of proteolytic enzyme that have different substrates, but which share similar structural characteristics [1,2,11,13,23]. fetched_contents.text: Research Progress on Bioactive Factors against Skin Aging Abstract The relentless pursuit of effective strategies against skin aging has led to significant interest in the role of bioactive factors, particularly secondary metabolites from natural sources. The purpose of this study is to meticulously explore and summarize the recent advancements in understanding and utilization of bioactive factors against skin aging, with a focus on their sources, mechanisms of action, and therapeutic potential. Skin, the largest organ of the body, directly interacts with the external environment, making it susceptible to aging influenced by factors such as UV radiation, pollution, and oxidative stress. Among various interventions, bioactive factors, including peptides, amino acids, and secondary metabolites, have shown promising anti-aging effects by modulating the biological pathways associated with skin integrity and youthfulness. This article provides a comprehensive overview of these bioactive compounds, emphasizing collagen peptides, antioxidants, and herbal extracts, and discusses their effectiveness in promoting collagen synthesis, enhancing skin barrier function, and mitigating the visible signs of aging. By presenting a synthesis of the current research, this study aims to highlight the therapeutic potential of these bioactive factors in developing innovative anti-aging skin care solutions, thereby contributing to the broader field of dermatological research and offering new perspectives for future studies. Our findings underscore the importance of the continued exploration of bioactive compounds for their potential to revolutionize anti-aging skin care and improve skin health and aesthetics. Keywords: skin aging, biological activity factor, oxidative stress, collagen, polypeptide, enzyme 1. Introudution Skin, as the body’s most direct organ in contact with the external environment [1,2], is not only a complex barrier organ [3] but also an intuitive manifestation of aging [4]. The degree of skin aging is not only a direct reflection of a person’s health status but has also been found to be an important indicator of predicting individual life expectancy [5]. Over time, skin can be affected by external and internal factors, such as light exposure, pollution, and disease, leading to aging. In the past, when discussing the causes and mechanisms of skin aging, it was found that oxidative stress theory, skin photoaging theory, inflammation theory, metabolism theory, etc., had a great influence on skin aging [6,7,8]. Because of the importance of oxidative stress in the skin aging process, most anti-skin-aging strategies and related products mainly focus on antioxidant defense. Previously, effective products were mainly derived from chemically extracted plant extracts and natural small molecule compounds. In recent years, with the development of biotechnology and the research progress on skin structure and its function in medicine, people have gained a deeper understanding of the factors affecting skin aging and related mechanisms. In fact, the loss or destruction of skin structural proteins/lipids/sugars or production disorders caused by various factors will directly lead to skin aging. In addition, organelles in skin cells and biological macromolecules, such as proteins, lipids, polysaccharides, and nucleic acids, can interact with each other, and this process can accelerate skin aging. Hyaluronan (HA) is a nonsulfated glycosaminoglycan that has been widely used in biomedical applications. HA treatment of cells can enhance cell viability. Specifically in atrophic stressed cells, effective drugs containing HA revealed a noteworthy beneficial effect on the myogenic biomarkers indicating that it could be used as a promising platform for tissue regeneration, with specific attention to muscle cell protection against stressful agents [9]. Skin cells can communicate with related cytokines through exosomes. Meanwhile, skin cells can interact with external microorganisms, and these skin microorganisms, in turn, can interact with each other in a manner that directly or indirectly influences skin oxidative stress or inflammation of tissues involved in the skin aging process. In conclusion, the primary aim of our study is to dissect the intricate role of bioactive factors, with a particular focus on secondary metabolites, in the fight against skin aging. As we delve into the realms of biotechnology and dermatological research, our understanding of the skin’s structural intricacies and functional dynamics continues to evolve, offering new horizons for anti-aging research. By compiling and summarizing recent advancements in the field, this study seeks not only to enrich the current academic discourse on skin aging and active ingredients but also to highlight potential pathways for the development of effective anti-aging interventions. Since many endogenous bioactive molecules, such as proteins, peptides, cytokines, and microbial metabolites, are themselves involved in the skin aging process, many bioactive components are directly used by pharmaceutical companies to develop relevant anti-skin-aging products. In addition, biological products also have the advantages of low environmental pollution, low side effects, high activity, specific targets, and easy biofabrication. fetched_contents.text: Recent advances in dermal fibroblast senescence and skin aging: unraveling mechanisms and pioneering therapeutic strategies Abstract Aging is a multifactorial process that affects skin integrity through the progressive decline of dermal fibroblast function. Dermal fibroblasts are key regulators of extracellular matrix (ECM) composition, wound healing, and tissue homeostasis. However, their dysfunction contributes to structural deterioration, chronic inflammation, and impaired regenerative capacity. Cellular senescence, a fundamental characteristic of aging, results in the buildup of senescent fibroblasts that release growth factors, matrix-degrading enzymes, and pro-inflammatory cytokines, known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). This study examines the impact of fibroblast senescence on dermal aging, highlighting mechanisms such as DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and telomere attrition. The role of SASP-driven ECM degradation, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) activation, and fibroblast-keratinocyte communication breakdown are explored, demonstrating their collective contribution to skin aging. Additionally, key signaling pathways, including p16INK4a/RB, p53, NF-κB, mTOR, and TGF-β, are implicated in fibroblast senescence and chronic inflammation. Recent advancements in therapeutic strategies targeting fibroblast aging, such as senolytics, extracellular vesicle-based interventions, and metabolic reprogramming, offer promising avenues for skin rejuvenation. This review delves into the molecular and cellular dynamics of dermal fibroblast aging, emphasizing their relevance for developing novel anti-aging interventions. Keywords: aging, dermal fibroblast, skin, SASP, signaling pathways 1 Introduction Aging is a multifaceted biological process characterized by the gradual deterioration of cellular and systemic functions, resulting in heightened vulnerability to diseases and an increased risk of mortality (Guo et al., 2022). At the cellular level, one of the hallmarks of aging is cellular senescence, a state of irreversible growth arrest triggered by various stressors, including DNA damage, telomere attrition, oxidative stress, and oncogenic signaling (López-Otín et al., 2023). Senescent cells, while initially beneficial in preventing the propagation of damaged cells, accumulate over time and contribute to chronic inflammation and tissue dysfunction through the release of growth factors, matrix-remodeling enzymes, and pro-inflammatory cytokines, known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) (Wang et al., 2024). This persistent low-grade inflammation, termed inflammaging, exacerbates age-related pathologies such as neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and cancer. Furthermore, mitochondrial dysfunction, epigenetic alterations, and impaired proteostasis also play critical roles in the aging process by disrupting cellular homeostasis (Srivastava, 2017; Wang K. et al., 2022). The skin is the largest organ of the human body, functioning as a highly specialized and dynamic barrier that protects against environmental insults, pathogens, and mechanical trauma while regulating thermoregulation and hydration (Kabashima et al., 2019; Gilaberte et al., 2016). Structurally, it comprises a complex interplay of epithelial, connective, and subcutaneous tissues, each contributing to its protective and homeostatic roles. The outermost layer consists of a continuously regenerating stratified squamous epithelium, primarily composed of keratinocytes, which form a resilient barrier against external stressors. Beneath this, a dense fibroblast-rich connective tissue network provides biomechanical strength and elasticity through extracellular matrix (ECM) components, such as collagen and elastin. The innermost layer is composed of adipose-rich subcutaneous tissue, functioning as an insulator and energy reserve while also aiding in shock absorption and metabolic regulation (Gilaberte et al., 2016; Richardson, 2003; Lee and Kim, 2022). However, intrinsic aging, driven by genetic and cellular factors, along with extrinsic factors such as ultraviolet (UV) radiation, pollution, and oxidative stress, leads to structural and functional deterioration (Farage et al., 2008; Hussein et al., 2025). Aged skin exhibits collagen degradation, reduced fibroblast activity, impaired wound healing, and increased senescence of dermal and epidermal cells, contributing to loss of elasticity, thinning, and the formation of wrinkles (Shin et al., 2019; Chin et al., 2023). The accumulation of senescent cells, particularly in the dermis, exacerbates chronic inflammation through the SASP, further accelerating aging-related skin degeneration (Figure 1) (Konstantinou et al., 2024). Given that dermal fibroblasts have a pivotal role in managing skin integrity by regulating ECM composition, wound healing, and cellular homeostasis, their dysfunction is a key driver of age-related skin deterioration. In this review, we examine the process of skin aging by focusing on the role of dermal fibroblasts, investigating their functional decline, ECM remodeling, and senescence-associated alterations that contribute to age-related structural and physiological deterioration. 2 The characteristics of dermal fibroblasts Dermal fibroblasts are mesenchymal cells specialized in preserving the skin’s structural framework and functional homeostasis. As the predominant cell type in the dermis, fibroblasts are responsible for the remodeling, synthesis, and degradation of the ECM, which provides the skin with mechanical strength, elasticity, and hydration (Plikus et al., 2021; Thulabandu et al., 2018). These cells primarily produce collagen (types I and III), glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), fibronectin, and elastin, ensuring the stability of the dermal-epidermal junction and facilitating skin repair and regeneration (Boraldi et al., 2024). Collagen-related mechanisms are central to anti-aging effects because collagen synthesis and degradation determine skin aging through structural integrity and matrix turnover. The evidence indicates that the extracellular matrix (ECM) is a macromolecular network composed of collagen, enzymes, and proteins, and that collagen is the most abundant protein in the ECM, providing structural support for cells [N2-F2]. Collagen is highly resistant to proteolysis, but only matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) can cleave it; the resistance and maintenance of collagen are tightly regulated by endogenous inhibitors such as TIMPs [N2-F2]. This means that aging-related skin changes are not just about collagen loss, but also about the balance between synthesis, degradation, and repair.

Collagen degradation is driven by MMPs, and MMPs are described as the main group of enzymes responsible for collagen and other protein degradation in the ECM [N2-R5]. The evidence also states that MMPs and their tissue inhibitors (TIMPs) regulate ECM dynamics, and that regulation of ECM dynamics is mediated by MMPs and TIMPs [N2-R2]. This directly supports the idea that anti-aging effects depend on controlling ECM turnover through these enzymes and their inhibitors. The search result on dermal fibroblast senescence and skin aging further frames this: aging fibroblasts reduce ECM formation, while senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) can drive ECM degradation, matrix metalloproteinases activation, and fibroblast-keratinocyte communication breakdown [N4-F4]. In other words, collagen-related aging is not a passive process; it is actively shaped by fibroblast senescence, SASP, and MMP activity.

The enzymes and signaling pathways regulating extracellular matrix turnover are therefore MMPs and TIMPs, with MMPs being the primary collagen-degrading proteases and TIMPs the primary endogenous inhibitors [N2-R2][N2-R5]. The mechanistic review also notes that MMPs are zinc-dependent endopeptidases with a conserved catalytic zinc site and that their activity is highly conserved across species [N2-F2]. In addition, the fibroblast aging evidence highlights key signaling pathways involved in fibroblast senescence and chronic inflammation, including p16INK4a/RB, p53, NF-κB, mTOR, and TGF-β [N4-F4]. These pathways are relevant because they control fibroblast function, senescence, and the secretion of matrix-remodeling enzymes and pro-inflammatory cytokines, which in turn affect ECM integrity [N4-F4]. The evidence therefore supports a multi-level regulatory system: extracellular enzymes (MMPs/TIMPs) and intracellular signaling pathways (p16INK4a/RB, p53, NF-κB, mTOR, TGF-β) both govern ECM turnover and aging-related ECM degradation [N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-F4].

Fibroblasts and matrix proteins contribute to skin resilience by regulating ECM composition, wound healing, and tissue homeostasis [N4-F4]. The fibroblast aging review states that dermal fibroblasts are key regulators of ECM composition, wound healing, and tissue homeostasis, and that their dysfunction contributes to structural deterioration, chronic inflammation, and impaired regenerative capacity [N4-F4]. Fibroblasts synthesize collagen types I and III, glycosaminoglycans, fibronectin, and elastin, and they maintain the stability of the dermal-epidermal junction [N4-F4]. The evidence also notes that aging fibroblasts reduce ELN and COL1A1 expression levels in surrounding fibroblasts, indicating that fibroblast senescence can weaken the ECM and reduce collagen synthesis [N4-R3]. This supports the idea that fibroblasts are not passive bystanders: they actively synthesize and remodel matrix proteins, and their senescence or dysfunction directly undermines skin resilience [N4-F4][N4-R3]. In aging skin, fragmented collagen fibrils and disrupted fibroblast-ECM interactions also reduce fibroblast function, further weakening skin structure [N4-R5].

Overall, the collagen-related mechanisms relevant to anti-aging effects are: collagen synthesis and degradation determine skin aging by maintaining ECM structure; MMPs and TIMPs regulate ECM turnover; and fibroblasts and matrix proteins contribute to skin resilience through synthesis, remodeling, and homeostasis [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-F4][N4-R3][N4-R5].

The evidence for anti-aging claims for fermented rice products is indirect and largely centered on bioactive factors rather than direct collagen-related outcomes in fermented rice itself. The search results indicate that fermented rice is discussed as a source of bioactive compounds, including organic acids, amino acids, polyphenols, vitamins, polysaccharides, and peptides [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1]. A review on bioactive peptides from fermented plant-based foods notes that fermented rice is one of the reviewed categories and that BAPs derived from fermented plant-based foods show promise of therapeutic benefits [N1-F1]. However, the evidence provided here does not identify any direct collagen-related outcomes specifically linked to fermented rice products in the search results. Instead, the evidence is more general: fermented rice products may contain bioactive compounds, and fermented foods derived from cereals can produce bioactive peptides with antioxidant, antihypertensive, antidiabetic, and immunomodulatory properties [N1-F1].

For fermented rice products, the strongest direct anti-aging evidence in the provided material is indirect: fermented rice has been reported to increase protein and total phenolic content in red rice, indicating that fermentation can amplify the production of beneficial compounds [N1-R5]. This supports the idea that fermentation can improve the bioactive profile of rice, but it does not directly link fermented rice products to collagen synthesis or degradation outcomes. The same review also states that fermented plant-based foods can increase the bioavailability of certain minerals from plant sources, including calcium, zinc, and iron, and that fermentation can enrich the pool of essential amino acids, vitamins, and minerals [N6-R2][N6-R4]. These findings suggest that fermented rice may improve nutrient availability, but they do not establish collagen-related anti-aging mechanisms.

The evidence in cell lines, animals, and humans is limited in the provided material. The most specific cell-line evidence comes from a study on Lactobacillus kefiri fermentation supernatant, which found that the product can delay aging of HSF at the biochemical, cellular, and molecular biology levels and can be utilized as a functional food ingredient [N3-R2]. This is relevant because it shows that fermented microbial supernatants can delay aging-related changes in cells, but it is not about rice fermentation specifically. A review on bioactive factors against skin aging states that collagen peptides, antioxidants, and herbal extracts have shown promising anti-aging effects by modulating biological pathways associated with skin integrity and youthfulness, and that bioactive factors can promote collagen synthesis and enhance skin barrier function [N3-F3]. However, this review is broader than fermented rice and does not provide direct evidence that fermented rice products achieve those effects.

The evidence in humans is also sparse. A synbiotic effects review on fermented rice notes that probiotic or synbiotic administration may help avoid or reduce high blood glucose levels in clinical research [N5-R1]. This indicates some human relevance for fermented rice-related interventions, but it is not about skin aging or collagen. Another result mentions a clinical trial focus on the safety of a drug, suggesting that safety studies exist for fermented rice products, but no direct anti-aging or collagen-related human trial is identified in the provided evidence [N5-R2]. A study on red yeast rice extract showed a statistically significant reduction in total cholesterol and LDL-C in people with hypercholesterolemia [N5-R3], but again, this is not about skin aging or collagen-related outcomes.

Limitations are substantial. First, the evidence does not show direct collagen-related outcomes from fermented rice products themselves; the strongest claims are about bioactive compounds and general anti-aging potential rather than collagen synthesis or degradation [N1-R5][N3-F3]. Second, the evidence is mostly preclinical or reviews, with limited human data on collagen-related outcomes [N3-F3][N5-R2]. Third, the studies referenced are not all about rice fermentation specifically; many are broader fermented foods or related bioactive compounds [N1-F1][N3-R2][N5-R1]. Fourth, study design and relevance to aging are uneven: some findings are in cell lines or animal models, others are human studies on metabolic outcomes rather than skin aging, and there is no direct evidence in the provided material that fermented rice products have been tested for collagen-related anti-aging effects in skin [N3-R2][N5-R2]. Overall, the evidence supports a plausible mechanism-based rationale for fermented rice products, but it does not yet provide strong direct evidence that they promote collagen-related anti-aging effects in the skin [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Rice fermentation products derive from rice and are enriched with bioactive components produced or released during fermentation. The provided evidence indicates that fermented rice is one of several fermented plant-based foods discussed in a review on bioactive peptides, and that fermentation can amplify the production of beneficial compounds such as organic acids, amino acids, polyphenols, polysaccharides, vitamins, and peptides [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1]. The same review notes that fermented foods-derived bioactive peptides (BAPs) have antihypertensive, antioxidant, and antibacterial activities, and that fermented rice is explicitly included among the reviewed categories [N1-F1]. A separate search result on fermented rice also states that fermentation can enrich the pool of essential amino acids, vitamins, and minerals and increases the overall quality of the product [N6-R2]. This suggests that rice fermentation products are not simply unfermented rice; fermentation alters the composition by increasing bioactive compounds and improving nutrient availability.

The major bioactive components likely present in rice fermentation products include peptides, amino acids, polyphenols, organic acids, polysaccharides, vitamins, and possibly other microbial metabolites [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1]. The review on bioactive peptides from fermented plant-based foods emphasizes that BAPs are defined by their distinct structural features and amino acid sequences and that they impart health benefits through antioxidant, antihypertensive, antidiabetic, and immunomodulatory properties [N1-F1]. This indicates that peptides are a key bioactive class, while polyphenols and other secondary metabolites are also likely to be present. Fermentation is also reported to increase protein and total phenolic content in red rice, supporting the idea that fermentation can enhance phenolic content [N1-R5]. The evidence further notes that fermented foods can produce antimicrobial peptides and other bioactive substances such as phenyl lactic acid, hydroxyphenyl acetic acid, indoleacetic acid, and alcohols [N1-F1], which suggests that fermentation may produce a broad spectrum of bioactive metabolites, not only peptides but also organic acids and other microbial-derived compounds.

The compounds most likely to affect collagen or related pathways are peptides, polyphenols, and other bioactive metabolites produced during fermentation, because these are the classes explicitly associated with antioxidant and bioactive properties [N1-F1][N1-R5]. The collagen-related mechanistic evidence provided elsewhere shows that matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) degrade collagen, TIMPs inhibit MMPs, and fibroblast senescence can drive ECM degradation and matrix-remodeling enzyme secretion [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-F4]. So any bioactive compound that modulates oxidative stress, inflammation, or proteolytic activity could plausibly influence collagen-related pathways. The review on bioactive factors against skin aging also highlights that collagen peptides, antioxidants, and herbal extracts have shown promising anti-aging effects by modulating pathways related to skin integrity and youthfulness, and that they can promote collagen synthesis and enhance skin barrier function [N3-F3]. This is relevant because it shows that compounds such as collagen peptides and antioxidants are already linked to collagen-related mechanisms in skin aging, and therefore fermentation-derived peptides and polyphenols may similarly influence those pathways [N3-F3].

Fermentation changes rice composition compared to unfermented rice by increasing bioactive compounds, enhancing nutrient availability, and enriching the pool of amino acids, vitamins, and minerals [N6-R2][N6-R4]. The evidence also suggests that fermentation can increase the bioavailability of minerals such as calcium, zinc, and iron in plant-based foods, and that fermented foods can reduce nondigestible carbohydrates while enriching the pool of essential nutrients [N6-R2][N6-R4]. In addition, the review on bioactive peptides states that fermentation can increase the synthesis of microbial metabolites with biological properties, and that fermentation may release bioactive compounds from the substrate [N1-F1]. This implies that fermentation not only preserves rice nutrients but also transforms them into more bioaccessible and bioactive forms. The fermentation of red rice is also cited as increasing protein and total phenolic content by 1.7 and 1.4 times, respectively, which demonstrates that fermentation can substantially alter the composition of rice [N1-R5]. 

Taken together, rice fermentation products contain peptides, amino acids, polyphenols, organic acids, polysaccharides, vitamins, and other microbial metabolites [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1][N1-R5]. These compounds may affect collagen-related pathways through antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, or proteolytic modulation, especially since fermentation increases bioactive compound content and bioavailability [N1-F1][N1-R5][N6-R2][N6-R4]. Fermentation changes rice composition by enriching nutrients, increasing bioactive compounds, and improving bioavailability [N6-R2][N6-R4][N1-R5].

The overall evidence supports a plausible mechanistic rationale for rice fermentation products promoting anti-aging effects through collagen-related mechanisms, but the clinical evidence is limited and uneven. Mechanistically, the evidence is strong and consistent: collagen is the most abundant protein in the extracellular matrix (ECM), and its synthesis and degradation determine skin aging [N2-F2]. Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) are the main collagen-degrading enzymes in the ECM, while TIMPs inhibit MMPs and regulate ECM dynamics [N2-R5][N2-R2]. Fibroblasts regulate ECM composition, wound healing, and tissue homeostasis, and their senescence can drive ECM degradation, matrix metalloproteinase activation, and SASP-driven remodeling [N4-F4]. This means that any compound affecting oxidative stress, inflammation, proteolytic activity, or fibroblast function could plausibly influence collagen-related aging [N2-F2][N2-R5][N4-F4].

The evidence for fermented rice products is therefore mechanistically plausible, but not yet strong. Rice fermentation products contain bioactive components such as peptides, amino acids, polyphenols, organic acids, polysaccharides, vitamins, and microbial metabolites [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1]. Fermentation can enrich amino acids, vitamins, minerals, and bioactive compounds, and can increase the bioavailability of certain minerals and nutrients [N6-R2][N6-R4][N1-R5]. These properties make it biologically plausible that fermented rice products could support skin resilience by modulating collagen-related pathways, especially since bioactive peptides and polyphenols are already associated with antioxidant and bioactive properties [N1-F1][N1-R5]. The review on bioactive factors against skin aging also notes that collagen peptides, antioxidants, and herbal extracts can promote collagen synthesis and enhance skin barrier function [N3-F3]. This provides a direct mechanistic bridge between fermented rice-derived bioactives and anti-aging skin effects.

However, direct evidence linking fermented rice products specifically to collagen-related outcomes is thin in the provided material. The strongest direct evidence is indirect: fermented rice can increase protein and phenolic content in red rice, but this does not show collagen synthesis or degradation effects [N1-R5]. The evidence for fermented rice products in humans is even more limited: the only human evidence cited is a synbiotic effects review suggesting fermented rice may help reduce high blood glucose levels, and a clinical trial focus on safety, not collagen-related skin aging [N5-R1][N5-R2]. A red yeast rice study showed cholesterol-lowering effects, but again, this is not about collagen or skin aging [N5-R3]. ## Integrated final answer: How rice fermentation products may affect collagen-related mechanisms to promote anti-aging effects

Rice fermentation products may support anti-aging effects through collagen-related mechanisms by altering the composition of rice and producing bioactive compounds that can influence collagen synthesis, degradation, and extracellular matrix (ECM) turnover. ### 1. Mechanistic pathway: collagen synthesis, degradation, and ECM regulation

Collagen is central to skin aging because it is the most abundant protein in the extracellular matrix and provides structural support for cells [N2-F2]. The evidence shows that collagen is highly resistant to proteolysis, but only matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) can cleave it, and TIMPs inhibit MMPs and regulate ECM dynamics [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R5]. This means that aging-related skin changes depend on the balance between collagen synthesis, degradation, and repair.

In aging skin, fragmented collagen fibrils and disrupted fibroblast-ECM interactions reduce fibroblast function, further weakening skin structure [N4-R5]. This supports the idea that fibroblasts and matrix proteins are not passive bystanders; they actively synthesize and remodel the ECM, and their dysfunction undermines skin resilience [N4-F4][N4-R3][N4-R5].

## Integrated final answer: How rice fermentation products may affect collagen-related mechanisms to promote anti-aging effects

Rice fermentation products may support anti-aging effects through collagen-related mechanisms by altering the composition of rice and producing bioactive compounds that can influence collagen synthesis, degradation, and extracellular matrix (ECM) turnover. The evidence suggests that these products are not simply unfermented rice; fermentation enriches them with peptides, amino acids, polyphenols, organic acids, polysaccharides, vitamins, and other microbial metabolites [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1]. This makes rice fermentation products biologically plausible candidates for affecting skin resilience and aging-related processes [N1-R2][N1-F1].

### 1. Mechanistic pathway: collagen synthesis, degradation, and ECM regulation

Collagen is central to skin aging because it is the most abundant protein in the extracellular matrix and provides structural support for cells [N2-F2]. The evidence shows that collagen is highly resistant to proteolysis, but only matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) can cleave it, and TIMPs inhibit MMPs and regulate ECM dynamics [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R5]. This means that aging-related skin changes depend on the balance between collagen synthesis, degradation, and repair.

The provided evidence also shows that fibroblasts regulate ECM composition, wound healing, and tissue homeostasis, and that fibroblast senescence can drive ECM degradation, matrix metalloproteinase activation, and SASP-driven remodeling [N4-F4]. In aging skin, fragmented collagen fibrils and disrupted fibroblast-ECM interactions reduce fibroblast function, further weakening skin structure [N4-R5]. This supports the idea that fibroblasts and matrix proteins are not passive bystanders; they actively synthesize and remodel the ECM, and their dysfunction undermines skin resilience [N4-F4][N4-R3][N4-R5].

### 2. How rice fermentation products may influence these mechanisms

The bioactive components likely to affect collagen-related pathways are peptides, polyphenols, and other microbial metabolites produced during fermentation [N1-F1][N1-R5]. Fermentation can increase protein and total phenolic content in red rice, indicating that fermentation can amplify the production of beneficial compounds [N1-R5]. The review on bioactive peptides from fermented plant-based foods emphasizes that BAPs are defined by structural features and amino acid sequences, and that they impart antioxidant, antihypertensive, antidiabetic, and immunomodulatory properties [N1-F1]. This is relevant because collagen-related aging is often driven by oxidative stress, inflammation, and proteolytic imbalance, and bioactive compounds may modulate these factors.

The evidence on fermentation also shows that fermentation can enrich the pool of essential amino acids, vitamins, and minerals, and can increase the bioavailability of certain minerals such as calcium, zinc, and iron [N6-R2][N6-R4]. This is important because bioavailability is a critical determinant of whether fermentation-derived compounds can reach concentrations sufficient to affect collagen-related pathways in vivo [N6-R2][N6-R4]. Fermentation may also reduce nondigestible carbohydrates and release bioactive compounds from the substrate, further supporting the idea that fermented rice products can deliver more bioaccessible and bioactive components than unfermented rice [N1-F1][N6-R2].

### 3. Plausible effects on collagen-related anti-aging

A plausible effect is that fermented rice products may improve skin resilience by supporting ECM integrity and reducing ECM degradation. The review on bioactive factors against skin aging notes that collagen peptides, antioxidants, and herbal extracts can promote collagen synthesis and enhance skin barrier function [N3-F3]. This provides a direct mechanistic bridge between bioactive compounds and anti-aging skin effects. Because fermented rice products contain bioactive peptides and polyphenols, they may plausibly modulate pathways that support collagen synthesis or reduce ECM degradation [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Another plausible effect is that fermentation-derived compounds may reduce oxidative stress and inflammation, both of which are linked to fibroblast senescence and ECM remodeling [N4-F4]. The fibroblast senescence review states that senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) can drive ECM degradation, matrix metalloproteinase activation, and fibroblast-keratinocyte communication breakdown [N4-F4]. If fermented rice products can reduce SASP activity or senescence-related inflammation, they may indirectly support skin resilience by preserving fibroblast function and ECM homeostasis [N4-F4].

### 4. Evidence for anti-aging claims

The evidence for fermented rice products specifically is indirect and mainly centered on bioactive factors rather than direct collagen-related outcomes in fermented rice itself [N1-R2][N1-F1]. The strongest direct evidence in the provided material is that fermentation can increase protein and phenolic content in red rice, but this does not show collagen synthesis or degradation effects [N1-R5]. The review on bioactive peptides also states that fermented plant-based foods can produce antimicrobial peptides and other bioactive substances, and that fermentation can increase the synthesis of microbial metabolites with biological properties [N1-F1]. These findings support a general anti-aging rationale but not a specific collagen-related claim.

Evidence in cell lines, animals, and humans is limited. A study on Lactobacillus kefiri fermentation supernatant found that the product can delay aging of HSF at the biochemical, cellular, and molecular biology levels and can be used as a functional food ingredient [N3-R2]. This is relevant because it shows that fermented microbial supernatants can delay aging-related changes in cells, but it is not about rice fermentation specifically. A review on bioactive factors against skin aging emphasizes that collagen peptides, antioxidants, and herbal extracts have shown promising anti-aging effects by modulating biological pathways associated with skin integrity and youthfulness [N3-F3]. However, this is broader than fermented rice products.

Human evidence is even more limited. A synbiotic effects review on fermented rice suggests that probiotic or synbiotic administration may help avoid or reduce high blood glucose levels in clinical research [N5-R1]. This indicates some human relevance for fermented rice-related interventions, but it is not about skin aging or collagen-related outcomes. A clinical trial focus on the safety of a drug suggests that safety studies exist for fermented rice products, but again, no direct anti-aging or collagen-related human trial is identified in the provided evidence [N5-R2]. A red yeast rice study showed a statistically significant reduction in total cholesterol and LDL-C in people with hypercholesterolemia [N5-R3], but this is unrelated to collagen or skin aging [N5-R3].

### 5. Strength of mechanistic versus clinical support

The mechanistic support is strong. The evidence shows that collagen synthesis and degradation determine skin aging, that MMPs and TIMPs regulate ECM turnover, and that fibroblasts and matrix proteins are central to skin resilience [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-F4]. It also shows that fermentation can increase bioactive compounds, improve bioavailability, and enrich amino acids, vitamins, and minerals [N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. These findings support a plausible mechanism by which rice fermentation products could influence collagen-related anti-aging effects.

The clinical support is weaker and more indirect. The evidence does not show direct collagen-related outcomes from fermented rice products in the provided material [N1-R5]. Instead, the strongest human evidence is related to metabolic outcomes or safety, not skin aging or collagen-related effects [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. This means the anti-aging claims are plausible, but they are not yet substantiated by strong clinical evidence.

### 6. Which effects are plausible versus overstated

Plausible effects include:
- improved bioactive compound content and bioavailability from fermented rice products [N1-R2][N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R4]
- reduced oxidative stress and inflammation, which may support fibroblast function and ECM homeostasis [N4-F4]
- indirect support for collagen synthesis or reduced ECM degradation via bioactive peptides and polyphenols [N1-F1][N3-F3]

Overstated claims would be:
- direct evidence that fermented rice products promote collagen synthesis or reduce collagen degradation in skin [N1-R5]
- generalization of metabolic effects to skin aging without skin-specific studies [N5-R1][N5-R2]
- claims that fermented rice products alone have been shown to produce strong anti-aging effects in skin [N5-R2][N1-R5]

### 7. Where more research is needed

More research is needed in several directions:
- direct studies on fermented rice products and collagen-related outcomes in skin, including cell lines, animals, and humans [N3-F3][N5-R2]
- mechanistic studies clarifying which bioactive compounds in fermented rice products affect MMPs, TIMPs, fibroblast senescence, or ECM remodeling [N2-F2][N2-R2][N4-F4]
- studies on bioavailability and dose-response relationships, because fermentation can increase bioactive content but does not guarantee sufficient concentrations to affect collagen-related pathways in vivo [N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R4]
- human trials specifically targeting skin aging, collagen synthesis, or extracellular matrix integrity rather than general metabolic outcomes [N5-R1][N5-R2]
- distinction between rice fermentation products and other fermented foods or microbial supernatants, since the provided evidence includes broader fermented foods and fermented rice is only one category [N1-F1][N3-R2]

### 8. Bottom line

Overall, the evidence suggests that rice fermentation products are biologically plausible candidates for promoting anti-aging effects through collagen-related mechanisms. They may affect these mechanisms by increasing bioactive compounds, improving bioavailability, and modulating oxidative stress, inflammation, and proteolytic activity [N1-R2][N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. However, the current evidence base is mainly mechanistic and indirect, and direct evidence linking fermented rice products specifically to collagen-related outcomes is thin [N1-R5]. The most reasonable conclusion is that the anti-aging claims are plausible but not yet substantiated, and that future research should focus on targeted mechanistic and clinical studies [N2-F2][N2-R2][N4-F4][N3-F3].

## Integrated final answer: How rice fermentation products may affect collagen-related mechanisms to promote anti-aging effects

Rice fermentation products may support anti-aging effects through collagen-related mechanisms by altering the composition of rice and producing bioactive compounds that can influence collagen synthesis, degradation, and extracellular matrix (ECM) turnover. The evidence suggests that these products are not simply unfermented rice; fermentation enriches them with peptides, amino acids, polyphenols, organic acids, polysaccharides, vitamins, and other microbial metabolites [N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1]. This makes rice fermentation products biologically plausible candidates for affecting skin resilience and aging-related processes [N1-R2][N1-F1].

### 1. Mechanistic pathway: collagen synthesis, degradation, and ECM regulation

Collagen is central to skin aging because it is the most abundant protein in the extracellular matrix and provides structural support for cells [N2-F2]. The evidence shows that collagen is highly resistant to proteolysis, but only matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) can cleave it, and TIMPs inhibit MMPs and regulate ECM dynamics [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R5]. This means that aging-related skin changes depend on the balance between collagen synthesis, degradation, and repair.

The provided evidence also shows that fibroblasts regulate ECM composition, wound healing, and tissue homeostasis, and that fibroblast senescence can drive ECM degradation, matrix metalloproteinase activation, and SASP-driven remodeling [N4-F4]. In aging skin, fragmented collagen fibrils and disrupted fibroblast-ECM interactions reduce fibroblast function, further weakening skin structure [N4-R5]. This supports the idea that fibroblasts and matrix proteins are not passive bystanders; they actively synthesize and remodel the ECM, and their dysfunction undermines skin resilience [N4-F4][N4-R3][N4-R5].

### 2. How rice fermentation products may influence these mechanisms

The bioactive components likely to affect collagen-related pathways are peptides, polyphenols, and other microbial metabolites produced during fermentation [N1-F1][N1-R5]. Fermentation can increase protein and total phenolic content in red rice, indicating that fermentation can amplify the production of beneficial compounds [N1-R5]. The review on bioactive peptides from fermented plant-based foods emphasizes that BAPs are defined by structural features and amino acid sequences, and that they impart antioxidant, antihypertensive, antidiabetic, and immunomodulatory properties [N1-F1]. This is relevant because collagen-related aging is often driven by oxidative stress, inflammation, and proteolytic imbalance, and bioactive compounds may modulate these factors.

The evidence on fermentation also shows that fermentation can enrich the pool of essential amino acids, vitamins, and minerals, and can increase the bioavailability of certain minerals such as calcium, zinc, and iron [N6-R2][N6-R4]. This is important because bioavailability is a critical determinant of whether fermentation-derived compounds can reach concentrations sufficient to affect collagen-related pathways in vivo [N6-R2][N6-R4]. Fermentation may also reduce nondigestible carbohydrates and release bioactive compounds from the substrate, further supporting the idea that fermented rice products can deliver more bioaccessible and bioactive components than unfermented rice [N1-F1][N6-R2].

### 3. Plausible effects on collagen-related anti-aging

A plausible effect is that fermented rice products may improve skin resilience by supporting ECM integrity and reducing ECM degradation. The review on bioactive factors against skin aging notes that collagen peptides, antioxidants, and herbal extracts can promote collagen synthesis and enhance skin barrier function [N3-F3]. This provides a direct mechanistic bridge between bioactive compounds and anti-aging skin effects. Because fermented rice products contain bioactive peptides and polyphenols, they may plausibly modulate pathways that support collagen synthesis or reduce ECM degradation [N1-F1][N3-F3].

Another plausible effect is that fermentation-derived compounds may reduce oxidative stress and inflammation, both of which are linked to fibroblast senescence and ECM remodeling [N4-F4]. The fibroblast senescence review states that senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) can drive ECM degradation, matrix metalloproteinase activation, and fibroblast-keratinocyte communication breakdown [N4-F4]. If fermented rice products can reduce SASP activity or senescence-related inflammation, they may indirectly support skin resilience by preserving fibroblast function and ECM homeostasis [N4-F4].

### 4. Evidence for anti-aging claims

The evidence for fermented rice products specifically is indirect and mainly centered on bioactive factors rather than direct collagen-related outcomes in fermented rice itself [N1-R2][N1-F1]. The strongest direct evidence in the provided material is that fermentation can increase protein and phenolic content in red rice, but this does not show collagen synthesis or degradation effects [N1-R5]. The review on bioactive peptides also states that fermented plant-based foods can produce antimicrobial peptides and other bioactive substances, and that fermentation can increase the synthesis of microbial metabolites with biological properties [N1-F1]. These findings support a general anti-aging rationale but not a specific collagen-related claim.

Evidence in cell lines, animals, and humans is limited. A study on Lactobacillus kefiri fermentation supernatant found that the product can delay aging of HSF at the biochemical, cellular, and molecular biology levels and can be used as a functional food ingredient [N3-R2]. This is relevant because it shows that fermented microbial supernatants can delay aging-related changes in cells, but it is not about rice fermentation specifically. A review on bioactive factors against skin aging emphasizes that collagen peptides, antioxidants, and herbal extracts have shown promising anti-aging effects by modulating biological pathways associated with skin integrity and youthfulness [N3-F3]. However, this is broader than fermented rice products.

Human evidence is even more limited. A synbiotic effects review on fermented rice suggests that probiotic or synbiotic administration may help avoid or reduce high blood glucose levels in clinical research [N5-R1]. This indicates some human relevance for fermented rice-related interventions, but it is not about skin aging or collagen-related outcomes. A clinical trial focus on the safety of a drug suggests that safety studies exist for fermented rice products, but again, no direct anti-aging or collagen-related human trial is identified in the provided evidence [N5-R2]. A red yeast rice study showed a statistically significant reduction in total cholesterol and LDL-C in people with hypercholesterolemia [N5-R3], but this is unrelated to collagen or skin aging [N5-R3].

### 5. Strength of mechanistic versus clinical support

The mechanistic support is strong. The evidence shows that collagen synthesis and degradation determine skin aging, that MMPs and TIMPs regulate ECM turnover, and that fibroblasts and matrix proteins are central to skin resilience [N2-F2][N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-F4]. It also shows that fermentation can increase bioactive compounds, improve bioavailability, and enrich amino acids, vitamins, and minerals [N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. These findings support a plausible mechanism by which rice fermentation products could influence collagen-related anti-aging effects.

The clinical support is weaker and more indirect. The evidence does not show direct collagen-related outcomes from fermented rice products in the provided material [N1-R5]. Instead, the strongest human evidence is related to metabolic outcomes or safety, not skin aging or collagen-related effects [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. This means the anti-aging claims are plausible, but they are not yet substantiated by strong clinical evidence.

### 6. Which effects are plausible versus overstated

Plausible effects include:
- improved bioactive compound content and bioavailability from fermented rice products [N1-R2][N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R4]
- reduced oxidative stress and inflammation, which may support fibroblast function and ECM homeostasis [N4-F4]
- indirect support for collagen synthesis or reduced ECM degradation via bioactive peptides and polyphenols [N1-F1][N3-F3]

Overstated claims would be:
- direct evidence that fermented rice products promote collagen synthesis or reduce collagen degradation in skin [N1-R5]
- generalization of metabolic effects to skin aging without skin-specific studies [N5-R1][N5-R2]
- claims that fermented rice products alone have been shown to produce strong anti-aging effects in skin [N5-R2][N1-R5]

### 7. Where more research is needed

More research is needed in several directions:
- direct studies on fermented rice products and collagen-related outcomes in skin, including cell lines, animals, and humans [N3-F3][N5-R2]
- mechanistic studies clarifying which bioactive compounds in fermented rice products affect MMPs, TIMPs, fibroblast senescence, or ECM remodeling [N2-F2][N2-R2][N4-F4]
- studies on bioavailability and dose-response relationships, because fermentation can increase bioactive content but does not guarantee sufficient concentrations to affect collagen-related pathways in vivo [N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R4]
- human trials specifically targeting skin aging, collagen synthesis, or extracellular matrix integrity rather than general metabolic outcomes [N5-R1][N5-R2]
- distinction between rice fermentation products and other fermented foods or microbial supernatants, since the provided evidence includes broader fermented foods and fermented rice is only one category [N1-F1][N3-R2]

### 8. Bottom line

Overall, the evidence suggests that rice fermentation products are biologically plausible candidates for promoting anti-aging effects through collagen-related mechanisms. They may affect these mechanisms by increasing bioactive compounds, improving bioavailability, and modulating oxidative stress, inflammation, and proteolytic activity [N1-R2][N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R4]. However, the current evidence base is mainly mechanistic and indirect, and direct evidence linking fermented rice products specifically to collagen-related outcomes is thin [N1-R5]. The most reasonable conclusion is that the anti-aging claims are plausible but not yet substantiated, and that future research should focus on targeted mechanistic and clinical studies [N2-F2][N2-R2][N4-F4][N3-F3].
